content: Desogestrel and Ethinyl Estradiol are oral contraceptives approved by the FDA for the prevention of unintended pregnancy in women who choose to use oral contraceptives as their method of contraception. Common side effects include chloasma (skin discoloration), weight changes, bloating, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, migraines, depression, amenorrhea (absence of menstruation), irregular bleeding, nipple discharge, menstrual disorders, vaginal bleeding, and breast swelling. To achieve maximum contraceptive effectiveness, the medication must be taken exactly as directed, without exceeding intervals of 24 hours between doses. The tablets are provided in a dispenser preset for a Sunday start, but a Day 1 start is also an option. For a Day 1 start, one rose-colored active tablet is taken daily from the first day of menstrual flow (Day 1) through Day 21 of the cycle. This is followed by one white reminder tablet daily for 7 days. After completing the 28 tablets, a new course begins the next day with a rose-colored active tablet. If the patient starts postpartum and is not breastfeeding, the medication can be initiated 4 weeks after delivery. However, the increased risk of thromboembolic disease during the postpartum period must be considered. If the patient has not had a period postpartum, an alternative contraceptive method should be used until 7 consecutive days of active tablets have been taken. Ovulation and conception prior to starting the medication should also be considered. If a patient misses one rose-colored active tablet during Weeks 1, 2, or 3, the missed tablet should be taken as soon as remembered. If two rose-colored active tablets are missed in Week 1 or Week 2, two tablets should be taken on the day remembered and two the next day, followed by one tablet daily until the pack is finished. A backup contraceptive method, such as condoms or spermicide, should be used for 7 days after missing pills. If two rose-colored active tablets are missed in Week 3, or if three or more active tablets are missed consecutively, the rest of the pack should be discarded, and a new pack should be started the same day. A backup contraceptive method should also be used for 7 days in this case. For a Sunday start, the first rose-colored active tablet is taken on the first Sunday after menstruation begins. If menstruation starts on a Sunday, the first active tablet is taken that day. If switching from another oral contraceptive, the first rose-colored active tablet should be taken on the first Sunday after the last active tablet of the previous product. Tablets are taken without interruption: one rose-colored active tablet daily for 21 days, followed by one white reminder tablet daily for 7 days. After completing 28 tablets, a new course begins the next day (Sunday). When starting a Sunday regimen, an alternative contraceptive method should be used until after the first 7 consecutive days of administration. Oral contraceptives are contraindicated in women with certain conditions, including thromboembolic disorders, a history of deep vein thrombophlebitis, known thrombophilic conditions, cerebrovascular or coronary artery disease, valvular heart disease with complications, persistent hypertension (>160 mmHg systolic or >100 mmHg diastolic), diabetes with vascular involvement, migraines with focal neurological symptoms, major surgery with prolonged immobilization, known or suspected breast carcinoma, endometrial carcinoma, estrogen-dependent neoplasia, undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding, cholestatic jaundice of pregnancy or jaundice with prior pill use, acute or chronic hepatic disease with abnormal liver function, hepatic adenomas or carcinomas, known or suspected pregnancy, or hypersensitivity to any component of the product. Cigarette smoking significantly increases the risk of serious cardiovascular events associated with combination oral contraceptive use, particularly in women over 35 years of age and with the number of cigarettes smoked. For this reason, combination oral contraceptives, including Apri®, should not be used by women over 35 who smoke. Oral contraceptives are associated with increased risks of myocardial infarction, thromboembolism, stroke, hepatic neoplasia, and gallbladder disease, although the risk of serious morbidity or mortality is very small in healthy women without underlying risk factors. However, the risk increases significantly in the presence of other risk factors such as hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and diabetes. The use of oral contraceptives has been associated with an increased risk of thromboembolic and thrombotic diseases. This risk is not related to the duration of use and disappears after discontinuation. Third-generation oral contraceptives, including those containing desogestrel, have been associated with a higher risk of venous thromboembolism compared to certain second-generation oral contraceptives. Studies suggest an approximate two-fold increased risk, corresponding to an additional 1 to 2 cases of venous thromboembolism per 10,000 women-years of use. However, some studies have not confirmed this increased risk. Oral contraceptives may also increase the risk of myocardial infarction, particularly in smokers or women with other risk factors for coronary artery disease, such as hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, obesity, and diabetes. The relative risk of heart attack for current oral contraceptive users has been estimated to be two to six times higher than for non-users, with the risk being very low in women under 30 years of age. Smoking in combination with oral contraceptive use has been shown to substantially contribute to the incidence of myocardial infarctions in women in their mid-thirties or older. Oral contraceptives have been shown to increase both the relative and attributable risks of cerebrovascular events, including thrombotic and hemorrhagic strokes. The risk is greatest among older hypertensive women who also smoke. A positive association has been observed between the amount of estrogen and progestogen in oral contraceptives and the risk of vascular disease. Oral contraceptives may also increase blood pressure and compound the effects of other cardiovascular risk factors, such as hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, age, and obesity. The use of oral contraceptives has been associated with an increased risk of benign hepatic adenomas, particularly after four or more years of use, especially with higher-dose formulations. Although rare, these tumors can rupture, leading to life-threatening complications.
